The cotton grown, spun and woven by farmers of the Indus valley, among the earliest anywhere in the world. Cotton was domesticated separately in the Old World and the Americas; in South Asia the tree cotton of the region was in use by the time of the Harappan civilisation.

The oldest trace comes from Mehrgarh in Pakistan, where cotton threads were found preserved inside a copper bead from the 6th millennium BCE. At Mohenjo-daro, scraps of cotton cloth dyed with madder red survive from the 3rd millennium BCE, along with many spindle whorls. Cotton cloth may have been among the goods carried to Mesopotamia, see Indus seals in Mesopotamia.

For thousands of years India led the world in cotton cloth. Herodotus wrote of Indian trees that grew wool finer than sheep's. Indian calicoes and muslins were traded across the Indian Ocean and later flooded Europe, until British mills, in the cotton revolution, learned to make cotton cloth by machine.
